title: If You Can't Win Open, Find a Cash Cow
documentTitle: Musk v. Altman (OpenAI) — Exhibit 59: Musk–Karpathy Email Chain on OpenAI Strategy
excerptForBlog:
Working at the cutting edge of AI is unfortunately expensive. For example, DeepMind's operating expenses in 2016 were at around $250M USD (does not include compute). With their growing team today it might be ~$1.5B/yr. But then Alphabet in 2016 reported ~20B net income so it's still fairly cheap even if DeepMind had no revenue of its own.

I also strongly suspect that compute horsepower will be necessary (and possibly even sufficient) to reach AGI. If historical trends are any indication, progress in AI is primarily driven by systems — compute, data, infrastructure. The core algorithms we use today have remained largely unchanged from the ~90s.

It seems to me that OpenAI today is burning cash and that the funding model cannot reach the scale to seriously compete with Google (an 800B company). If you can't seriously compete but continue to do research in open, you might in fact be making things worse and helping them out 'for free', because any advances are fairly easy for them to copy and immediately incorporate, at scale.

The most promising option I can think of would be for OpenAI to attach to Tesla as its cash cow. Using a rocket analogy, Tesla already built the 'first stage' of the rocket with the whole supply chain of Model 3. The 'second stage' would be a full self-driving solution based on large-scale neural network training, which OpenAI expertise could significantly help accelerate. I cannot see anything else that has the potential to reach sustainable Google-scale capital within a decade. —Andrej

Elon Musk forwarded this to OpenAI leadership, adding: 'Andrej is exactly right. Tesla is the only path that could even hope to hold a candle to Google.'

lessonTitle: If You Can't Win Open, Find a Cash Cow
pullQuote: Open research without a profit engine isn't idealism — it's free R&D for whoever has the bigger bank account.
leadershipTraits: willing to break founding principles for survival
sequences big bets like an engineer
situation: In early 2018, Andrej Karpathy sent Elon Musk a strategic memo arguing that OpenAI's nonprofit funding model couldn't compete with Google at scale. Karpathy estimated DeepMind alone was running at roughly $1.5 billion per year in operating expenses, while OpenAI was 'burning cash' with no comparable revenue engine. Musk forwarded the memo to OpenAI leadership with a single line of endorsement.
insight:
Karpathy's core argument is a capital sufficiency problem, not a talent or research problem. He writes that 'the funding model cannot reach the scale to seriously compete with Google' — and then takes it one step further. Open research under those conditions might actively hurt OpenAI, because Google can 'copy and immediately incorporate, at scale' any advances OpenAI publishes for free. That's a classic platform asymmetry trap: you do the R&D, the entrenched giant absorbs it at zero marginal cost.

His proposed fix is a **Build vs. Buy pivot toward vertical integration** — attach OpenAI's research capability to Tesla's cash-generating hardware business, specifically full self-driving, which he calls the 'second stage' rocket using Tesla's Model 3 supply chain as the first. The logic: Tesla is the only entity outside Big Tech that could generate Google-scale capital within a decade. Musk's one-line endorsement — 'Tesla is the only path that could even hope to hold a candle to Google' — signals he already agreed with the diagnosis. Whether the solution was ever executable is beyond what this document shows.
application: Map your funding ceiling against your biggest competitor's operating budget — right now, with real numbers. If the gap is structural (they have a profit engine; you have donors or early-stage investors), don't just raise another round. Ask which existing cash-flow business your core capability could accelerate, and whether attaching to it is faster than building your own revenue from scratch.
